speaker: Brian Potter
title: Construction Physics Author Brian Potter - Why America Struggles to Build
question: In large commercial aircraft manufacturing, why has the global market persisted as a two-company duopoly for decades?
guest: The aircraft industry is just so small in terms of the number of airplanes sold a year. For a large commercial aircraft like a Boeing 737, the market only sells maybe 1,000 to 1,500 of those a year, so there isn't much room to carve up the market among many participants. At the same time, it's extraordinarily expensive to develop and build a new model of aircraft, partly because of safety and partly because you have to test it so much. You have to earn back those huge upfront costs over a certain number of sales. If the market is carved up too much, there just isn't enough market share to go around. What you saw in the '70s, '80s, and '90s was more competitors getting slowly whittled down because developing these aircraft was so expensive. For example, Lockheed competed in commercial aircraft with the TriStar—it cost them billions of dollars to develop, they only sold a tiny number, and they lost huge amounts of money on it.

points.core: Global annual unit sales of large commercial airliners are surprisingly small.

points.note: Accept: fragmenting a small unit market across three or more OEMs leaves insufficient volume per firm, driving exits (e.g., Lockheed, McDonnell Douglas). Do not credit: attributing the duopoly purely to government protectionism or airline brand loyalty.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The Boeing–Airbus duopoly persists because the barriers to entry are extraordinarily high and mutually reinforcing.

Developing a new airliner costs tens of billions of dollars and takes a decade or more, with payback only after hundreds of deliveries, so a single failed program can bankrupt a company. The market is too small to support many players at that scale: steep learning curves and economies of scale mean unit costs fall sharply with cumulative production, giving incumbents a cost advantage that a newcomer cannot match on early aircraft.

Incumbency also locks in customers. Airlines value fleet commonality (shared pilot training, spare parts and maintenance), a proven safety record, strong resale values and a global support network, all of which a new entrant lacks. Certification is demanding and slow, and the supply chain and engineering expertise are concentrated around the two incumbents.

Finally, both companies have been sustained by government support (launch aid, defence contracts, tax breaks), making them effectively too strategic to fail. Earlier rivals such as McDonnell Douglas and Lockheed merged or exited, and challengers like China's COMAC, Russia's UAC and Bombardier's C Series (now the Airbus A220) have struggled or been absorbed.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
The large commercial aircraft market has remained a duopoly between Boeing and Airbus because extraordinary financial, regulatory, and operational barriers prevent newcomers from reaching viable scale. Developing a single new jetliner requires $15 billion to $30 billion in upfront investment and roughly a decade before generating revenue, creating massive economies of scale and steep manufacturing learning curves where unit costs fall only after hundreds of deliveries.

Entrants must also clear years of stringent safety certification from regulators like the FAA and EASA, without which airlines cannot fly internationally or secure affordable financing from lessors who demand proven reliability and predictable resale values. Furthermore, airlines face steep switching costs: fleet commonality across pilot training, maintenance, spare parts, and global repair networks strongly favors incumbents. Decades of industry consolidation, state backing, defense synergies, and tightly integrated global supplier networks further entrench both firms. Even heavily subsidized challengers like China’s COMAC still depend on Western subsystems and lack global certification and support infrastructure—leaving a market where airlines sustain two suppliers to preserve pricing leverage, yet economics deter a third.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer: Boeing and Airbus have held onto the market mostly because of the industry's economics, with politics reinforcing them. A new airliner program costs $10–30 billion or more and takes about a decade before the first delivery. Each aircraft is only profitable after hundreds of sales, so production volume and the learning curve decide unit costs, and a market that can support only a few products ends up with very few players. Certification by the FAA and EASA is slow and expensive, and new entrants struggle with it, as COMAC's C919 shows. Airlines also have strong reasons to stick with what they fly, because standardized fleets, pilot type ratings, spare parts, maintenance networks and decades of support make switching costly. Buyers also need long reliability records and financing that residual-value guarantees can back, which favors established brands. Governments treat both firms as national strategic assets, giving them launch aid, defense contracts and export credit, so they are effectively too important to fail. Past rivals such as McDonnell Douglas and Lockheed left or merged, and Airbus absorbed Bombardier's C Series. These barriers keep new competition marginal, though China's COMAC is slowly trying to break in.

The large commercial aircraft market has remained a duopoly between Boeing and Airbus because its economics create nearly insurmountable barriers to entry. Designing, testing, and certifying a clean-sheet jetliner requires tens of billions of dollars in upfront, sunk development costs and a decade or more to break even. Given the finite global demand for large jets, only a few manufacturers can achieve the production volumes needed to spread these fixed costs profitably.

Incumbents also benefit from steep learning curves in managing extraordinarily complex global supply chains, steadily lowering unit costs with experience. Meanwhile, airlines face high switching costs: fleet commonality minimizes pilot training, spare-parts inventories, and maintenance expenses, making carriers reluctant to bet on unproven newcomers lacking worldwide support networks. Finally, stringent safety certification regimes and decades of government backing—through defense contracts, research subsidies, and export financing—have reinforced Boeing and Airbus’s dominance, leaving state-backed challengers like China’s COMAC struggling to gain international certification and scale.

Boeing and Airbus have remained dominant because a new manufacturer has to spend billions of dollars and years developing, testing, and certifying an aircraft before delivering a single plane. It then needs hundreds of orders to spread those costs, plus the suppliers, production capacity, and global service network to keep aircraft flying for decades.

Airlines also have reasons to stick with manufacturers they already use. Related aircraft can share pilot training, maintenance procedures, and spare parts. An entrant must persuade airlines and leasing companies that it can deliver on schedule, support the fleet worldwide, and build enough demand for the aircraft to retain its resale value. That creates a catch-22: buyers want proof of scale before committing, but the manufacturer needs their orders to reach scale.

Airbus broke into the market with sustained European government backing, while other Western producers merged or exited. Today, Boeing and Airbus each have enough global demand to sustain a broad product line, and airlines benefit from having two suppliers compete for their business.

Airbus and Boeing have dominated the market for large commercial jets because a new manufacturer must spend billions of dollars and years designing, testing, and certifying an aircraft before it can deliver one. It then needs enough orders to spread those costs across a long production run. Both companies already have the factories, experienced suppliers, and global maintenance networks to build and support aircraft at scale.

Airlines reinforce that advantage. Buying another jet from a familiar aircraft family can reduce pilot training costs, simplify spare-parts inventories, and limit downtime. A newcomer therefore has to offer enough value to justify those switching costs while convincing airlines it can deliver on schedule and support the jet for decades.

Government backing helped Airbus reach the scale needed to challenge Boeing, while consolidation narrowed the field of established manufacturers. The result is a durable duopoly, though the entry of China’s COMAC shows that it is still possible to challenge it.
